title: Demand doubled in one city and supply did not follow
summary: Growth in one market is breaking the experience for both sides. The obvious lever is the one that makes it worse.

brief.role: You are the PM for the marketplace core team.
brief.company: Thistle, a marketplace connecting people with vetted home-repair tradespeople in 14 cities.
brief.context: Manchester was your third city and has been healthy for two years. Over the last four months a well-received local press feature and a referral promotion have roughly doubled demand there. Supply — the number of active tradespeople — has grown 11% in the same period. Job acceptance times have gone from a median of 40 minutes to 4 hours, 23% of jobs now go unaccepted for 24 hours, and customer ratings in Manchester have fallen from 4.7 to 4.3. The growth team wants to keep spending, since Manchester customer acquisition cost is the lowest in the network. Your head of marketplace has asked you what to do before the next city launch takes the team's attention.
brief.objective: Restore a healthy marketplace in Manchester without permanently damaging either side of it.
brief.constraints: Four engineers and one operations coordinator dedicated to Manchester for up to six weeks. Supply acquisition is run by a separate team with its own targets. Pricing changes need commercial sign-off.
brief.task: Decide what you do about the imbalance and explain the mechanism you are relying on.

evidenceCards.title: Marketplace health data
evidenceCards.content:
Manchester, four months ago → now:
- Jobs posted per week: 1,180 → 2,340
- Active tradespeople (accepted ≥1 job in 30 days): 412 → 458
- Median time to acceptance: 40 min → 4h 10m
- Jobs unaccepted after 24h: 4% → 23%
- Customer rating (completed jobs): 4.7 → 4.3
- Tradesperson-side: jobs accepted per active tradesperson per week 2.6 → 4.4
- Tradesperson churn (active, then inactive 30 days): 3.1%/month → 5.8%/month

Job mix, four months ago → now:
- Emergency/same-day: 22% → 19%
- Scheduled small jobs (under £150): 41% → 58%
- Scheduled large jobs (over £150): 37% → 23%

Network comparison: in the other 13 cities, jobs per active tradesperson per week ranges from 2.1 to 3.2. Manchester is now well outside that.

evidenceCards.title: Tradesperson interviews and behaviour
evidenceCards.content:
Nine interviews with Manchester tradespeople, including three who recently went inactive.

- All nine described the job feed as 'noisy' now. Several said they used to check it a few times a day and now 'it's a firehose and most of it isn't worth my time'.
- The three who went inactive all cited small jobs: 'I'd scroll past forty £80 jobs to find one worth driving for.' Two of the three still work through a competitor.
- Six said they now only look at the feed in the evening, in a batch, rather than through the day. This matches the acceptance-time data.
- Four raised travel: the referral promotion brought in customers from outlying areas, and jobs 30-40 minutes away at £80 are not economic.
- One said something the researcher flagged: 'You've got more work than you've got tradesmen. Everyone knows it. Nobody's raised what we get paid.'

Operations coordinator's note: 'Our vetting takes 3-4 weeks per tradesperson and we're at capacity. Even if acquisition doubled tomorrow, supply moves in months, not weeks.'

evidenceCards.title: Customer behaviour and economics
evidenceCards.content:
Customer acquisition cost in Manchester: £14, network average £38. The referral promotion accounts for roughly 60% of the new demand; the press feature accounts for most of the rest.

Customers whose job goes unaccepted for 24h: 61% do not post again within 90 days. Customers whose job is accepted within an hour: 34% post again within 90 days.

Take rate is 12% of job value, flat across job sizes. So a £80 job earns £9.60 and a £400 job earns £48.

Contribution by job size, Manchester, last month: small jobs (58% of volume) produced 31% of revenue; large jobs (23% of volume) produced 54%.

Commercial note: a Manchester-only take-rate or pricing change is technically possible but has not been done before in the network, and the commercial lead is wary of 'city-specific pricing we then have to explain'.

evidenceCards.title: What the team could build
evidenceCards.content:
Engineering estimates for Manchester-deployable changes:

- Feed filtering and relevance: let tradespeople filter by job value, distance and category, and rank the feed by fit rather than recency. Three weeks. Deployable network-wide afterwards.
- Push notifications for high-fit jobs: one week, depends on the relevance work.
- Minimum job value or a small-job surcharge: two weeks to build, needs commercial sign-off, and changes what customers pay.
- Slowing demand: pausing the referral promotion in Manchester is an operations action, not engineering. Effect within a week.
- Batching small jobs geographically (offer three nearby small jobs as one route): six weeks, novel, and the operations coordinator thinks it may not match how tradespeople plan their days.
- Supply acquisition: not this team's to run, but the marketplace lead could ask for Manchester priority. Vetting capacity is the binding constraint, not lead volume.

decisionPrompt: What do you do about Manchester over the next six weeks?

decisionOptions.label: Build feed relevance and pause the referral promotion
decisionOptions.description: Spend three weeks on filtering and fit-ranking so tradespeople can find worthwhile jobs, and pause the Manchester referral promotion immediately to stop adding demand the market cannot absorb.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Pausing the promotion cuts weekly job postings from 2,340 to roughly 1,700 within two weeks. Acceptance time improves to about 1h 40m before any engineering ships, simply from the reduced volume.
Feed relevance and high-fit notifications ship in week four. Median acceptance falls to 55 minutes; unaccepted-at-24h drops from 23% to 7%. Tradesperson churn returns to 3.4%/month over the following two months, and two of the three inactive interviewees return.
The growth team is unhappy about pausing the cheapest acquisition in the network, and says so. Manchester customer ratings recover to 4.6 over the quarter.
The relevance work is deployed network-wide the following quarter and improves acceptance times in four other cities.
Trade-off: you turned off cheap growth for a quarter and built a matching improvement rather than adding supply, which is still the underlying shortage.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strongest when the rationale identifies that the problem is matching quality plus demand volume, that supply cannot respond within the window because of vetting capacity, and that unaccepted jobs destroy demand (61% do not return) — so cheap acquisition into a broken market is not cheap.

decisionOptions.label: Keep spending and push supply acquisition hard
decisionOptions.description: Manchester CAC is £14 against a network average of £38. Keep the demand and ask the supply team to prioritise Manchester recruitment.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The supply team reprioritises. Manchester tradesperson leads triple within three weeks, but vetting capacity is the constraint and active supply grows from 458 to 501 over three months.
Meanwhile demand keeps growing. Unaccepted-at-24h reaches 29%, ratings fall to 4.1, and tradesperson churn rises to 6.9%/month — the market is losing supply almost as fast as it adds it.
Because 61% of customers with an unaccepted job do not return, the effective cost of a retained Manchester customer rises well above the £14 headline. When someone finally computes it, it is closer to £46.
Trade-off: you optimised the metric that looked best and spent a quarter acquiring customers the marketplace could not serve.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Weak. CAC is only cheap if acquired customers are served; the 61% non-return figure converts the headline into a much higher effective cost. It also ignores the vetting bottleneck that makes supply unresponsive within the window.

decisionOptions.label: Change the economics of small jobs
decisionOptions.description: Introduce a Manchester minimum job value or small-job surcharge so that the £80 jobs clogging the feed either become economic or stop being posted.
decisionOptions.consequence:
After three weeks of commercial debate, a £15 small-job surcharge ships in Manchester. Small-job volume falls from 58% to 44% of postings. Acceptance time improves to about 2h 20m.
Customer complaints about the surcharge appear immediately, and the commercial lead's fear is realised: the support team fields questions about why Manchester costs more. Two local press mentions are negative.
Tradesperson sentiment improves — the feed is less noisy — but the underlying matching problem remains, so tradespeople still scroll to find fit.
Trade-off: you addressed the job mix directly and paid for it in customer trust and a pricing precedent the network now has to manage.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: A real lever aimed at a real cause. Credit for identifying the small-job mix shift. Mark down when the rationale does not weigh that a filtering change achieves much of the same effect without changing what customers pay.

decisionOptions.label: Build small-job batching
decisionOptions.description: Solve the small-job economics with product: bundle three nearby small jobs into one route so they become worth accepting.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The work takes seven weeks rather than six. Adoption is low — 14% of eligible tradespeople try it, 6% use it more than once. The operations coordinator's doubt turns out to be right: most tradespeople schedule around customer availability, not around routes, so pre-bundled jobs conflict with their own calendars.
During those seven weeks nothing else changed. Unaccepted-at-24h stays above 20% and tradesperson churn stays near 6%.
The idea is sound in principle and is revisited a year later with scheduling flexibility built in, where it works better.
Trade-off: you attacked the most interesting version of the problem and spent the entire window on the least certain intervention.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Low. The operations coordinator's doubt was available before committing, and it consumes the whole window on a novel mechanism while cheaper, more certain levers exist.

rubric.referenceReasoning: Two things changed at once and only one of them is a supply shortage. Demand doubled, but the job mix also shifted heavily toward small jobs (41% → 58%), and the tradesperson interviews say the feed became unusable rather than merely busy — six of nine now batch-check it in the evening, which is exactly the acceptance-time pattern in the data. So a large part of the damage is a matching problem that filtering and fit-ranking can address in three weeks. Supply cannot respond in the window regardless: vetting takes 3-4 weeks per person and is at capacity, so acquisition effort does not convert to active supply inside six weeks. Meanwhile the cheap CAC is an illusion while 23% of jobs go unaccepted, because 61% of those customers never return; buying more demand into a market that cannot serve it destroys both sides at once. The strong move is therefore to stop adding demand temporarily, fix matching, and let supply catch up — while being honest that this does not solve the underlying supply gap, only the acute failure.
evidenceSignals: Notices the job mix shifted toward small jobs, not only that volume doubled
Connects the evening batch-checking behaviour to the four-hour acceptance time
Uses the 61% non-return rate for unaccepted jobs to reframe the £14 CAC
Identifies vetting capacity, not lead volume, as the supply bottleneck
Notes Manchester is far outside the network's normal jobs-per-tradesperson range
Sees that tradesperson churn rising to 5.8% means the market is losing supply while demand grows

product_sense: Diagnoses a matching problem alongside the supply imbalance rather than only the imbalance
Recognises that both sides of a marketplace are being damaged simultaneously
Treats reducing demand as a legitimate product action rather than a failure
analytics: Reframes CAC in terms of retained customers rather than acquired ones
Uses the network-wide jobs-per-tradesperson range as a health benchmark
Separates the volume change from the mix change
user_research: Uses the interviews to explain why acceptance time rose, not just that it did
Takes the operations coordinator's doubt about batching seriously
prioritization: Chooses interventions that fit inside the window over ones that cannot
Notices the relevance work is reusable across the network
execution: Sequences an immediate operational action ahead of a three-week build
Recognises supply acquisition cannot respond inside six weeks and plans accordingly
communication: Gives the growth team a specific, quantified reason the cheap CAC is not cheap
Is explicit that the intervention does not solve the underlying supply gap

product_sense: Treats the problem as purely 'not enough supply' and ignores the mix and matching changes
Optimises for the customer side while supply churn accelerates
analytics: Takes the £14 CAC at face value while 23% of jobs go unaccepted
Ignores that supply grew 11% while demand grew 98%
user_research: Ignores the interview evidence about feed noise and evening batching
prioritization: Commits the whole window to the most novel and least certain option
Relies on supply acquisition inside a window where vetting makes it impossible
execution: Has no immediate action while a multi-week build proceeds
communication: Does not address the growth team's incentive or give them a reason to accept a pause

learnTakeaway.title: In a marketplace, cheap demand is only cheap if you can serve it
learnTakeaway.body: Acquisition cost is a per-acquisition number; marketplace health is a per-match number. When 23% of jobs go unaccepted and 61% of those customers never return, a £14 CAC is really a £46 cost per retained customer — and the same imbalance is simultaneously driving away the supply that would fix it. Marketplaces fail on both sides at once, so reducing demand is a legitimate lever, and matching quality is often a faster one than adding supply, which usually moves on a hiring or vetting clock you do not control.

qaSubmissions.label: strong
qaSubmissions.rationale: Two things changed and only one is a supply shortage. Demand doubled, but the mix went 41% to 58% small jobs, and the interviews say the feed stopped being usable — six of nine now check it once in the evening, which is exactly the four-hour acceptance time. Supply can't help inside this window: vetting is 3-4 weeks and at capacity, and churn at 5.8% means we're losing supply while we wait. So pause the referral promotion now, the only lever that acts in a week, and build feed relevance. For growth I have a number: 61% of unaccepted-job customers never return, so £14 CAC is nearer £46.

qaSubmissions.label: defensible_alternative
qaSubmissions.rationale: I'd go at the small-job economics with a Manchester minimum job value and accept the commercial friction. The mix shift is what tradespeople actually describe: scrolling past forty £80 jobs, and jobs 30-40 minutes out that aren't economic at any level of feed quality. Filtering makes those jobs easier to skip; it doesn't make them get done. Small jobs are 58% of volume and 31% of revenue. I'd frame it as a travel-and-callout minimum and pause the promotion at the same time. The weakness: pricing needs three weeks of sign-off, and filtering could have shipped by then.

qaSubmissions.label: weak
qaSubmissions.rationale: Manchester CAC is £14 versus £38 network average, which is by far our most efficient market, so I would not slow down demand. The real problem is that we have not grown supply fast enough — 11% against roughly 100% demand growth. I would ask the supply team to make Manchester their top priority and recruit aggressively until the ratio is back in line.
